    PROTEST OF BIRCH CREEK DEVELOPMENT LLC TO ENTERGY’S JUNE 5, 2026,
             DEFICIENCY RESPONSE AND AMENDED WDAT FILING

        Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy
Regulatory Commission (“Commission” or “FERC”) and the Commission’s June 5, 2026 notice
of filing, Birch Creek Development, LLC (“Birch Creek”) hereby submits this protest to the June
5, 2026, deficiency response and amended filing by Entergy Services, LLC, 1 on behalf of Entergy
Arkansas, LLC (“EAL” or “Entergy Arkansas”), Entergy Louisiana, LLC (“ELL” or “Entergy
Louisiana”), Entergy Mississippi, LLC (“EML” or “Entergy Mississippi”), Entergy New Orleans,
LLC (“ENOL” or “Entergy New Orleans”), and Entergy Texas, Inc. (“ETI” or “Entergy Texas”)
(collectively, “Entergy” or the “Entergy Operating Companies”) in the above-captioned
proceeding (the “Deficiency Response” or “Amended Filing”).

        Entergy’s Deficiency Response confirms and compounds the fundamental deficiencies that
Birch Creek identified in its March 20, 2026, protest, reinforcing the need for hearing and
settlement judge proceedings. Entergy acknowledges in the Deficiency Response that the original
filing contained multiple workpaper errors, affecting the stated rates for every Entergy Operating
Company. These errors stemmed from an entire spectrum of root causes, including switched cell
values, incorrect functional-rate calculations that excluded sub-rate-class revenues, and erroneous
cell references that overstated rates. The magnitude of the resulting rate changes, with individual
operating company rates shifting by as much as 63 percent, demonstrates that the original filing
was not supportable and that Entergy’s proposed rates require the scrutiny that hearing and
settlement judge procedures will provide.

                          I. BACKGROUND AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY

        On February 27, 2026, Entergy Services, LLC, on behalf of the Entergy Operating
Companies, filed a proposed Wholesale Distribution Access Tariff (“WDAT” or “WD Access
Tariff”) and form Wholesale Distribution Access Service Agreement (“WDA Service
Agreement”) in the above-captioned docket. The proposed WDAT would establish the rates,

 terms, and conditions pursuant to which owners and operators of Distributed Energy Resources
(“DER”) and Energy Storage Systems (“ESS”) connected to the Entergy Operating Companies’
distribution systems may utilize those systems to deliver energy to the Midcontinent Independent
System Operator, Inc. (“MISO”) Transmission System and/or receive energy from the MISO
Transmission System to charge an ESS.

         On March 20, 2026, Birch Creek filed an intervention and protest demonstrating that the
Entergy Filing was patently deficient because did not include the cost-of-service information
required for rate changes under the Commission’s regulations, supporting testimony, or an officer
attestation, and proposed rates and tariff terms that raised serious concerns about justness and
reasonableness. On the same date, Azimuth Renewables, LLC, filed a separate protest raising
similar concerns. On April 6, 2026, Entergy filed an answer to the protests.

         On April 29, 2026, Commission staff issued a deficiency letter that confirmed the filing
was deficient and directed Entergy to provide detailed additional information regarding, among
other things: (1) a narrative explanation of cost-support information and methodology; (2) the
appropriateness of using billing determinants and unit costs from different years; (3) the
appropriateness of the functionalization methodology; (4) rate-class selection; (5) an officer
attestation; (6) the basis for denying service “in its sole discretion” for unstated “other reasons”;
(7) the alignment of creditworthiness provisions with Order No. 890; and (8) the financial impact
analysis for termination costs. The Deficiency Letter expressly stated that the “information
requested in this letter will constitute an amendment to your filing, and a new filing date will be
established.”2

        On June 5, 2026, Entergy filed its Deficiency Response, which admitted and corrected
multiple workpaper errors, submitted an Amended Exhibit 1 with revised rate calculations,
proposed amendments to certain tariff terms and conditions, and submitted clean and marked
versions of an Amended WD Access Tariff. The Deficiency Response acknowledged material
errors in the original workpapers including but not limited to: (a) inadvertently switched average
demand charge values in the EAL Rates tab; (b) inadvertent exclusion of sub-rate-class revenues
from the General Service Rate Class functional-rate calculation for Entergy Louisiana; and (c) use
of incorrect cell references from the Large General Service rate class in calculating the High Load
Factor Service functional rates for Entergy Louisiana, which resulted in an overstated primary-
voltage rate. Entergy renewed its request for an effective date of May 1, 2026.

    II. ENTERGY’S ERRORS AND MATERIAL RATE REVISIONS REINFORCE THE
          NEED FOR HEARING AND SETTLEMENT JUDGE PROCEEDINGS

        Entergy’s Deficiency Response admits multiple workpaper errors that fundamentally
undermine the reliability of the filing and the rates proposed for acceptance effective May 1, 2026.
The nature and magnitude of these errors, together with the filing’s continuing non-compliance
with Commission regulations, demonstrate that the proposed rates must be further evaluated in
hearing and settlement judge proceedings before being accepted. In Attachment 1 to this
submission, Birch Creek offers expert analysis from Black and Veatch’s Dr. Albert Bremser
regarding Entergy’s submissions. In his sworn affidavit and exhibits, Dr. Bremser analyzes
Entergy’s proposed rate, its response to the Deficiency Letter, and the data sources used by Entergy
in calculating the rate. He concludes that Entergy’s submission continues to be deficient and non-
compliant with the Commission’s requirements.

        Entergy admits material errors in the original Exhibit 1 workpapers which result in
changes to the proposed rates for every operating company at all voltage levels. The following
table compares the rates stated in the original filing to the amended rates proposed in the
Deficiency Response.

        As illustrated in the table and discussed by Dr. Bremser, the revisions are material. At
one end of the spectrum, the Entergy Louisiana primary-voltage rate decreased by 63.5 percent,
while the Entergy Arkansas primary-voltage rate increased by 21.5 percent. Rate changes of this
magnitude across every operating company at every voltage level illustrate that the rate model
involves important factual and methodological judgments. These are exactly the kinds of issues
that hearing and settlement judge procedures are designed to resolve, and they confirm that the
amended rates should not be accepted on a summary basis without further evidentiary
development.

        Birch Creek does not suggest that Entergy acted in bad faith in preparing its original
workpapers. However, the breadth and nature of the corrections, spanning multiple operating
companies and involving computational references, sub-rate-class revenue inclusions, and
functional-rate calculations, raise reasonable questions that must be addressed through further
proceedings. As Dr. Bremser explains, the information and data provided by Entergy in this
proceeding to date does not provide sufficient information to establish whether the proposed
rates and rate designs are consistent with the Commission’s principles, practices, and
requirements, nor whether the retail rate schedules and functionalization studies utilized by
Entergy are an appropriate basis to calculate the proposed rates or reasonably reflect the costs of
providing wholesale distribution service. 3

        Hearing and settlement judge procedures will allow the parties and the Commission to
verify the corrected calculations, test the assumptions driving the amended rates, and determine
whether the resulting rates appropriately reflect the cost of providing wholesale distribution
access service to DER and ESS customers. The Commission has long held that “all rate
applicants have an affirmative obligation to adequately support their rate applications.” 4
Likewise, a utility proposing to utilize retail rates in determining rates for Commission-
jurisdictional wholesale distribution service “must adequately demonstrate how the retail rates
accepted by the [state commission] are the basis for the wholesale rates in question and
reasonably reflect the cost of providing the service at issue.” 5 Setting this matter for hearing and
settlement judge proceedings will ensure that these obligations are fully discharged here.

            III. THE AMENDED RATES ARE STILL NOT JUST AND REASONABLE

A. Entergy Louisiana’s Rates Are Not Adequately Supported

        Entergy’s Deficiency Response acknowledges that Entergy Louisiana’s retail base rates
“have not been comprehensively reset through a fully litigated retail rate case in over 25 years” 6
and that the Unit Cost study underlying the ELL rate calculation dates from 2002. Entergy
further acknowledges that it paired this antiquated Unit Cost study with 2022 billing
determinants from a more recent filing, a filing that was resolved through settlement without
resetting base rates. This combined approach may ultimately be explainable, but it presents
significant factual issues that should be tested in hearing and settlement judge procedures before
being used to establish a generally applicable wholesale distribution access rate.

        The Commission's ratemaking standards require that rates be based on reasonably current
and reliable cost data. A functionalization methodology derived from a 2002 Unit Cost study
should be examined carefully before it is used to apportion costs among production,
transmission, and distribution functions for 2026 wholesale distribution access service.
Moreover, Entergy's justification for this approach depends on the premise that the 2002 Unit
Cost study remains the most appropriate source because no fully litigated rate case has reset base
rates. That may explain Entergy’s choice, but it does not by itself demonstrate that the resulting
wholesale rate is just and reasonable for FERC-jurisdictional service. The absence of a
comprehensive, current retail rate case heightens the need for this Commission to examine the
underlying cost allocation and rate design before accepting the proposed rates.

B. The Rate-Class Selection Remains Conclusory and Unsupported

        Commission Staff specific directed Entergy to “explain why the specific rate classes were
included in the rate calculation for each Entergy Operating Company,” but Entergy’s response
remains conclusory and provides no empirical evidence demonstrating that wholesale DER and
ESS customers are comparable to the retail commercial and industrial rate classes used as proxies.
Entergy states only that it selected rate schedules that are “currently available to new customers,”
“contain explicit demand charges,” and are “representative of the general commercial and
industrial customer characteristics expected of potential WD Access Tariff customers.” 7 It
provides no meaningful analysis to support these assertions.

        DER and ESS facilities seeking wholesale distribution access service are fundamentally
different from retail commercial and industrial load-serving customers. A solar generating facility
or battery storage system that injects power onto the distribution system and delivers it to the MISO
transmission system does not “use” the distribution system in the manner or with the load

6
    Deficiency Response at pg. 6.
7

4898-6780-2692.1
 characteristics of a retail customer that consumes electricity to power a factory or office building.
The directional flow of power, the coincidence of demand with system peak, the diversity of load,
and the duration of service are all materially different. Entergy has provided no load studies,
demand profiles, or other empirical comparison to demonstrate that retail commercial and
industrial billing determinants provide a reasonable proxy for the cost of serving wholesale
DER/ESS access customers. The only demonstrated commonality is that Entergy charges these
customers on a demand basis, as it proposes to charge under the WDAT.

        The Commission should not accept rates derived from retail rate classes that bear no
demonstrated resemblance to the wholesale customers who will actually take service under the
WDAT. Without empirical evidence of comparability, the proposed rate-class selection is
arbitrary and the resulting rates are not shown to be just and reasonable.

C. Formula Rate Plan Adjustments Are Not Adequately Supported

       For those Entergy Operating Companies utilizing Formula Rate Plans (“FRPs”), Entergy’s
methodology applies “the most current approved FRP adjustments” to update distribution-only
rates to “current effective levels.”8 While the Deficiency Response provides additional
transparency regarding the FRP adjustment mechanics, it does not demonstrate that applying retail
FRP riders, which are designed to adjust total bundled retail rates for changes in total revenue
requirements, to an isolated distribution-only component produces just and reasonable wholesale
rates.

        FRP adjustments at the retail level are calculated on a system-wide basis encompassing all
cost functions. Applying such an adjustment factor to a distribution-only rate assumes that
distribution costs change at the same rate as total system costs, an assumption that may not hold
and that Entergy has not verified. If, for example, transmission or generation costs have increased
disproportionately since the base rate case, applying the total FRP adjustment to the distribution
component would overstate the distribution-only rate. Entergy has not provided the granular,
function-specific cost data necessary to validate this approach.

D. The Functionalization Methodology Remains Insufficiently Proven

        Although Entergy has refined its functionalization methodology in the Amended Exhibit
1 to perform calculations at the voltage-specific level rather than the rate-class level,
fundamental issues persist. The methodology still relies on proportional cost allocations from
Unit Cost studies that may not be appropriate and were developed for retail ratemaking purposes
that may not align with FERC cost-of-service ratemaking principles. Subtracting production and
transmission percentages from a bundled average rate to arrive at a distribution residual assumes
that each Unit Cost study’s three-way split of costs reasonably reflects current conditions.

 Entergy’s methodology also assumes that the distribution portion of costs paid by certain retail
customer classes is a reasonable proxy for the costs caused by DER/ESS wholesale access
customers. These assumptions, and the related cost inputs, have significant impacts on the
resulting rates and should be tested through hearing and settlement judge procedures.

     IV. THE FILING CONSTITUTES A RATE CHANGE SUBJECT TO 18 C.F.R. § 35.13

         Entergy’s initial filing acknowledged that the Entergy Operating Companies maintain an
existing Wholesale Distribution Service Tariff (“Existing WDS Tariff”) on file with the
Commission in Docket No. ER19-858-000. Entergy’s filing further stated that, following
acceptance of the proposed WDAT, Entergy “will file to amend the existing WDS Tariff to limit
availability to entities that serve load” and that the WDAT “will be the mechanism for DER and
ESS to obtain distribution service to access MISO markets.” 9 This filing therefore is not a “new”
tariff being offered alongside continued availability of existing service at existing rates. Rather, it
is a filing that, by Entergy’s own design, will supersede and restrict the availability of the existing
wholesale distribution service tariff for DER and ESS customers.

       Section 35.13 of the Commission’s regulations applies whenever a public utility files “all
or part of a rate schedule, tariff, or service agreement to supersede or otherwise change the
provisions of a rate schedule, tariff, or service agreement filed with the Commission[.]” 10 “The
Commission’s long-standing precedent is that an initial rate filing is one which provides for [1] a
new service [2] to a new customer, and that both the service and the customer must be new.” 11

         Because the proposed WDAT, by Entergy’s own admission, will become the exclusive
mechanism for DER and ESS wholesale distribution access, displacing the Existing WDS Tariff
for this class of customers, it does not provide a new service and fails criteria one of the “initial
rate” test. Accordingly, Entergy’s filing constitutes a change in rate schedules subject to Section
35.13’s full filing requirements. Entergy cannot avoid Section 35.13 by nominally characterizing
its filing as a “new” tariff while simultaneously planning to restrict access to the existing tariff
once the new one is accepted. The functional effect is identical to amending the Existing WDS
Tariff to impose different rates, terms, and conditions on DER and ESS customers that would
currently be served under the Existing WDS Tariff. The Commission should therefore evaluate
this filing under the full requirements of Section 35.13, including the requirements for cost-of-
service information (Section 35.13(d)), supporting testimony (Section 35.13(e)), and information
regarding the effect of the rate change (Section 35.13(c)).

         As Birch Creek demonstrated in its March 20, 2026, protest, and as the Deficiency Letter
confirmed by requesting extensive additional information, the filing does not include Statements
AA through BM, prepared testimony, an adequate explanation of the rate change’s effect, or (until
the Deficiency Response) even an officer attestation. The Deficiency Response’s provision of
certain narrative explanations and amended workpapers does not cure these deficiencies; narrative
responses to Staff questions are not a substitute for the structured cost-of-service submissions that
Section 35.13 requires. Entergy’s amended filing continues to fail to satisfy the Commission’s
requirements.

  V. PERMITTING ENTERGY’S PROPOSED RATES TO BECOME EFFECTIVE AS
 REQUESTED WOULD CONSTIUTE PROHIBITED RETROACTIVE RATEMAKING

       The Commission’s April 29, 2026, Deficiency Letter unambiguously stated that the
“information requested in this letter will constitute an amendment to your filing, and a new filing
date will be established.”12

        Entergy’s Deficiency Response asks the Commission to maintain the originally-requested
effective date of May 1, 2026. This request should be denied. The Deficiency Response was filed
on June 5, 2026. Under the Commission’s standard notice requirements, the earliest permissible
effective date cannot be earlier than 60 days after the new filing date, i.e., no earlier than August
4, 2026.

        Even if Entergy had requested waiver of the Commission’s prior notice requirements in
the Deficiency Response/Amended Filing, which it did not, the date of the Deficiency Response
(the new filing date) would be the earliest possible effective date without violating the rule against
retroactive ratemaking. Accordingly, the Commission should deny Entergy’s request for
retroactive effectiveness.

                              VI. REMAINING NON-RATE DEFICIENCIES

       While Entergy has made certain amendments to the WDAT’s non-rate terms and
conditions in response to the Deficiency Letter, deficiencies persist that render the tariff unjust,
unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory.

A. Sole Discretion to Deny Service

        The amended tariff deletes the phrase “or other reasons” from the denial-of-service
language in Section V.B, which addresses one aspect of Birch Creek’s and Staff’s concerns.
However, the tariff retains language permitting Entergy to deny service based on its “sole
discretion.” The Commission has consistently held that vesting a utility with sole and


12
     Deficiency Letter at pg. 6.
                                            Page 8 of 10
4898-6780-2692.1
 unreviewable discretion to deny service is inconsistent with the open-access principles underlying
wholesale tariffs. The appropriate standard is “reasonable discretion” or a defined set of objective
criteria, not unfettered sole discretion. The retention of “sole discretion” language continues to
afford Entergy the ability to deny service for pretextual or discriminatory reasons without
meaningful recourse for the denied applicant.

B. Creditworthiness Provisions Remain Deficient

        In response to Staff's question regarding alignment with Order No. 890’s creditworthiness
requirements, Entergy has replaced the off-website “Entergy Creditworthiness Requirements”
definition with a new “Entergy Security Requirement” that cross-references Order No. 890. While
this is a constructive revision, the amended tariff does not, but should, 13 set out the specific
creditworthiness standards that will apply. Order No. 890 established a framework for establishing
acceptable creditworthiness provisions, including requirements for transparent criteria, objective
standards, and non-discriminatory application, but it is not self-executing and requires Entergy to
set forth the criteria and standards that will be applied. Customers should be able to determine
from the tariff the credit evaluation criteria, acceptable forms of security, deposit requirements,
and procedures that will apply to them, in order to ensure that credit standards are transparent,
comparable, and applied on a non-discriminatory basis.

C. Termination-Cost Provision Remains Inadequate

        The amended tariff's Section 3.4 of Attachment B now provides that Entergy will furnish
the terminating customer with a draft invoice for review and comment before issuing a final
invoice. This is an improvement over the original provision. However, Entergy's narrative
response to Question 8 describes a more robust standard than what is reflected in the tariff text.
The transmittal letter suggests that termination costs would be limited by a cost-causation
standard and that a system-benefit offset would apply. The filed tariff text, however, provides
only for a draft invoice and a requirement that both parties “use commercially reasonable efforts
to mitigate costs.” To the extent Entergy intends for these customer protections to apply, they
should be stated in the tariff so that they are enforceable and transparent.

D. Asymmetric Indemnification and Liability Provisions

       The WDAT's indemnification and liability provisions remain asymmetric, imposing
substantial indemnification obligations on WDA Service Customers while limiting the Entergy
Operating Companies’ exposure. Birch Creek respectfully submits that these provisions should

 be reviewed in hearing and settlement judge procedures to determine whether a more balanced
allocation of indemnification obligations and liability limitations is appropriate for this
standardized FERC-jurisdictional service.

                                     VII. REQUESTED RELIEF

For the foregoing reasons, Birch Creek respectfully requests that the Commission:

           (a) suspend the tariff for the maximum five-month period from the new filing date;

           (b) make the tariff effective subject to refund upon conclusion of the suspension period;

           (c) establish hearing and settlement judge procedures, and

           (d) deny Entergy’s request for retroactive effectiveness to May 1, 2026.

                                         VIII. CONCLUSION

        Entergy’s June 5, 2026, Deficiency Response and amended WDAT filing provide
additional information but confirm that significant factual and methodological issues remain to be
resolved in further proceedings. The admitted workpaper errors, which affected every operating
company and caused rate changes as large as 63.5 percent, demonstrate that the rate proposal
should be tested in further proceedings. As discussed herein and in Dr. Bremser’s analysis,
Entergy has not satisfied the Commission’s requirements for changes in rates under Section 35.13,
and the amended rates continue to raise substantial questions regarding the use of retail customer
classes as proxies for DER/ESS cost causation, the application of FRP adjustments, and the
functionalization methodologies used to isolate distribution-related costs. Several non-rate tariff
terms also warrant further refinement.
